worlds.setting: Surrey and London in an Edwardian June, a few years after 1900. The narrator is a writer on philosophy living near Woking; his brother is a medical student in London. Mars is an older, cooling world whose inhabitants, all brain and hands, have watched Earth for generations. Their cylinders fall on commons and heaths in the Home Counties, and the story follows the two brothers through the collapse of the most powerful city on Earth.
worlds.conflict: Beings as far above humanity as humanity is above animals arrive with heat-rays, poison smoke and three-legged fighting-machines, and the British army cannot stop them. There is no hero and no plan: the narrator hides, flees and watches, and the invaders are finally killed by bacteria, the smallest things on Earth.
worlds.politics: The empire at the height of its confidence, facing what it did to Tasmania done to itself. Government dissolves within days: the army is broken, London empties, and people become refugees on their own roads. An artilleryman the narrator meets imagines a new society living in the drains; the narrator does not join him.
worlds.technology: Victorian England's best: railways, telegraphs, field artillery and the ironclad Thunder Child. Against it the Martians bring the Heat-Ray, the Black Smoke, tripod fighting-machines, handling-machines and a flying-machine, all worked by creatures who feed by injecting human blood.
worlds.mood: Calm, reportorial and appalled; a story of ordinary roads and villages told as if it happened last week.

worlds.setting: The United States twenty and twenty-five years after a fungal infection turned most of its people into violent hosts. A few cities survive as walled quarantine zones under a military government; outside them the suburbs, highways and downtowns are overgrown and full of the infected. Small towns like Jackson, Wyoming run themselves behind their own walls, and the rest of the country belongs to smugglers, militias, cults and raiders.
worlds.conflict: Survival is the constant, but the story turns on what people will do to one another for those they love. A smuggler is paid to carry an immune girl to the rebels who want to make a vaccine from her, and chooses her over the cure; years later the surgeon's daughter comes for him, and the revenge that follows runs from Wyoming to Seattle to the California coast.
worlds.politics: The military government, FEDRA, holds the quarantine zones by curfew, rationing and summary execution; the Fireflies are an armed resistance that wants the old government back. After the military withdraws, militias and sects take the cities: the Washington Liberation Front in Seattle, the Seraphites against them, the Rattlers keeping slaves in Santa Barbara. Jackson is a self-governing town of a few hundred.
worlds.technology: Present-day technology running down: guns, improvised bombs, salvaged cars, generators and a hydroelectric dam that Jackson keeps turning. There is no working national network, no mass medicine and no vaccine; the only research effort, the Fireflies' hospital in Salt Lake City, ends in 2034.
worlds.mood: Quiet, brutal and intimate. Long stretches of overgrown silence broken by sudden violence, and a story that keeps asking whether love for one person can justify harm to everyone else.

worlds.setting: Britain after the Rage virus, a disease that turns people into frenzied killers within moments of infection. In the first weeks London is empty and the army holds a few roadblocks; seven months later American-led troops try to resettle a corner of the capital. Twenty-eight years on the mainland is overgrown and still infected, the country is sealed off from a Europe that recovered, and small communities live where the water protects them.
worlds.conflict: The infected are the constant threat, but each film finds the worse danger in the uninfected: soldiers who want the women, an army ordered to kill everyone in a failing safe zone, gangs and cults that rule the empty mainland. Against them stand ordinary people trying to keep a family alive, and a doctor who thinks the infected might be people still.
worlds.politics: The British state is gone within a month. In 28 Weeks Later a US-led NATO force governs the resettlement zone under military rule. By 2030 Britain is under indefinite international quarantine, patrolled from the sea; the Lindisfarne community governs itself, and on the mainland power belongs to whoever is armed.
worlds.technology: Early-2000s Britain, frozen and decaying: petrol cars, radios, army hardware, and in 2003 NATO snipers, helicopters and firebombs. By 2030 the islanders use bows and scavenged tools; the only medicine is what a lone doctor can find, and there is no vaccine or cure.
worlds.mood: Fast, raw and frightening in the first two films, shot on digital video in real London streets; the later films are stranger and more mournful, about memory, grief and what a country becomes when the world stops waiting for it.

worlds.setting: The United States in the summer and autumn after a weaponised flu from a secret Army laboratory kills more than ninety-nine people in a hundred. Cities are silent and full of the dead, the power is off and the roads are blocked with abandoned cars. The few thousand survivors drift across the country, drawn by dreams either to an old woman in Nebraska who leads them to Boulder, Colorado, or to a dark man gathering followers in Las Vegas.
worlds.conflict: A contest between good and evil played out by ordinary people. Boulder's Free Zone tries to rebuild a democratic town with committees and a power plant; Randall Flagg rules Las Vegas by fear and crucifixion and is gathering weapons. The survivors must decide whom they belong to, and four men from Boulder walk west to stand against him.
worlds.politics: The federal government collapses within weeks after trying to hide the plague and spreading it abroad. The Boulder Free Zone governs itself through public meetings and an elected committee; Las Vegas is a one-man tyranny with efficient services and public executions. Beyond the two camps there are only stragglers and small gangs.
worlds.technology: The United States of 1980, with no one left to run it: cars, guns, radios, a power station Boulder has to restart, and military stockpiles in the desert, including the nuclear warhead that ends Las Vegas.
worlds.mood: Sprawling, colloquial and apocalyptic: a road novel and a religious allegory, with long stretches of American small-town life overtaken by horror, and a stubborn belief in decency.
themes: the arrogance of the military state

worlds.setting: A Los Angeles suburb between 1976 and 1979, after a war and a plague. Everyone Robert Neville knew is dead or has come back as a vampire. By day the streets are empty and he drives among abandoned houses to hunt, scavenge and read; by night the undead gather outside his boarded-up house calling his name. Dust storms still blow, and he has no idea whether anyone else is alive.
worlds.conflict: Neville against loneliness first and the vampires second. He fortifies his house, kills the sleeping undead by day and turns to science to understand the plague. The real contest is revealed late: a new society of the living infected is rising, and to them the man who has been killing their people in their sleep is the monster.
worlds.politics: No state survives the plague. The government's last acts are orders to burn the dead. By 1978 the living infected have organised a new society with its own squads, rules and medicine, and they intend to clear the city of both the undead and Neville.
worlds.technology: 1950s America projected into the late 1970s: a generator, a car, a record player, stakes, garlic and mirrors, and a microscope and library Neville uses to teach himself bacteriology. The new society's only technology shown is a pill that holds the germ in check.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic, grieving and bleak, with bursts of rage and drink; a novel about loneliness more than horror, ending in a reversal that makes the hero the monster.
themes: a new species replacing the old

worlds.setting: A North America of the coming century where biotech corporations rule. Their scientists live in walled compounds with private police; everyone else lives in the crowded, violent pleeblands. The climate has turned, the coasts are flooding, and the shops sell spliced animals, lab-grown meat and pills for everything. After the Waterless Flood the same landscape is empty, hot and overgrown, patrolled by pigoons and wolvogs, and home to the gentle Crakers.
worlds.conflict: Before the Flood: two schoolfriends from the compounds, Jimmy, who likes words, and Crake, who designs life, and the woman they both love, while a sect of Gardeners and a cell of bioterrorists resist the corporations. After it: the few survivors, the Crakers and the pigoons must decide whether they can live together, while two sadistic Painballers hunt them.
worlds.politics: Government has been hollowed out: corporations own the compounds and the CorpSeCorps, their security force, does the policing, surveillance and disappearing. Dissent survives only as religion (the God's Gardeners) and sabotage (the MaddAddam network). After the Flood a few dozen survivors govern themselves by discussion and, at the end, by trial.
worlds.technology: Mature genetic engineering: pigs that grow human organs, bioengineered pets, chicken meat grown without heads, and Crake's Crakers, humans redesigned to be peaceful, herbivorous and seasonal breeders. The internet serves execution and suicide shows. The BlyssPluss pill carries the virus that ends it all.
worlds.mood: Darkly funny, satirical and elegiac; a lonely man talking to himself on a beach, interleaved with a coming-of-age story in a world selling itself to death, and in the later books a stubborn, earthy hope.

worlds.setting: London in 1984, or about then, the chief city of Airstrip One, a province of Oceania, which covers the Americas, the British Isles, Australasia and southern Africa. The city is shabby and bomb-damaged, with rotting nineteenth-century houses under four huge white Ministries. Telescreens watch every Party member at home and at work. Oceania is always at war with one of the other two superstates, Eurasia and Eastasia, and always allied with the other.
worlds.conflict: Winston Smith rewrites old newspapers for the Ministry of Truth and privately hates the Party. He keeps a diary, has an affair with Julia, and looks for the Brotherhood, the resistance run by the Party's official enemy, Goldstein. O'Brien, the man he trusts, is Thought Police. The Party's aim is not just to punish him but to make him believe whatever it says.
worlds.politics: Ingsoc (English Socialism) is a one-party oligarchy: a small Inner Party, a larger Outer Party of functionaries, and the proles, 85 per cent of the population, left alone in poverty. Big Brother is its face and may not exist. The four Ministries are Truth (propaganda), Peace (war), Love (police and torture) and Plenty (rationing). The permanent war uses up surplus production and justifies the emergency.
worlds.technology: Deliberately stalled, apart from war and surveillance. Two-way telescreens, hidden microphones, speakwrites, pneumatic tubes and memory holes that feed the Records Department's furnaces, Floating Fortresses, rocket bombs falling on London, and the atomic bomb that all three powers stockpile but have not used since the war. Newspeak, a language being cut down so that dissent cannot be put into words.
worlds.mood: Grey, cold and airless: gin, boiled cabbage and fear, with brief warmth in a rented room above an antique shop, then the long, clinical cruelty of the Ministry of Love.
themes: control of the past as control of the present

worlds.setting: London and its outskirts in AF 632, about 2540, six centuries into a World State that dates its calendar from Henry Ford. People are grown in bottles at the Central London Hatchery, sorted before birth into castes from Alpha to Epsilon, and conditioned to love their place. Everyone is kept busy with work, sport, casual sex and the drug soma. Outside the state are the Savage Reservations, such as the one in New Mexico, where people still give birth, marry and grow old.
worlds.conflict: Bernard Marx, an Alpha who does not fit, brings John the Savage from the Reservation to London. John was raised on an old volume of Shakespeare and cannot accept a world that has traded art, religion, love and suffering for stability. The book's real argument is the long debate between John and Mustapha Mond, the Controller who knows exactly what was given up and why.
worlds.politics: Ten World Controllers rule a peaceful, stable world state. Caste, consumption and pleasure are engineered, and dissent is handled by exile to islands, not by prisons. The motto is 'Community, Identity, Stability'. The past, the family and old religion have been abolished, but the Controllers keep forbidden books in their safes.
worlds.technology: Ectogenesis and Bokanovsky's Process, which makes up to ninety-six identical twins from one egg. Hypnopaedia and Neo-Pavlovian conditioning. Soma. Feelies, films with touch as well as sound. Rocket planes and helicopters for the upper castes. Science itself is kept under control, because real discovery would threaten stability.
worlds.mood: Bright, clean and sterile, a satire that turns into tragedy: the jokes are about happiness, and the ending is a man alone in a lighthouse.
themes: the abolition of the family and the past

worlds.setting: Panem, the nation that replaced North America after rising seas, droughts, fires and a war for food. The Capitol is a rich city in the Rockies. It rules twelve fenced, impoverished districts, each producing one thing: coal for District 12 in Appalachia, grain for 11, textiles for 8, masonry and Peacekeepers for 2. District 13 was supposedly destroyed in the Dark Days rebellion. Every year each district gives up two children to the televised Hunger Games.
worlds.conflict: Katniss Everdeen volunteers for the 74th Games to save her sister and wins by refusing to kill her fellow tribute, Peeta. That refusal sets off unrest that President Snow cannot contain. The Quarter Quell, District 13's war and the fall of the Capitol follow. The prequels show how Snow built the Games into a spectacle, and how Haymitch's defiance at the 50th Games was buried.
worlds.politics: A capital-and-colonies dictatorship under President Snow, enforced by Peacekeepers, starvation and the Games, which are both punishment and entertainment. District 13, the hidden rival, is a militarised bunker state under President Coin. After the war Commander Paylor of District 8 leads a new republic.
worlds.technology: Capitol luxury alongside district poverty: hovercraft, force fields, engineered arenas and weather, genetically made 'muttations' such as tracker jackers and jabberjays, surgical cosmetics, and total control of broadcasting. District 12 mines coal with little more than picks and lamps.
worlds.mood: Tense and first-person, told as a survival story that becomes a war story. The spectacle is always on and every image is propaganda, and the ending is quiet and scarred.
themes: propaganda and who controls the image
the cost of revolution to those who fight it

worlds.setting: London in 1997-98, ten years after a nuclear war that destroyed Europe and Africa and left Britain flooded, hungry and alone. Norsefire, a fascist party allied with the surviving corporations, runs the country through departments named after body parts. The Finger is the secret police, the Eye and Ear watch and listen, the Nose investigates and the Mouth broadcasts. They are joined through Fate, a computer the Leader worships. worlds.conflict: V, a masked survivor of the Larkhill camp, spends a year killing the people who ran it and destroying the regime's symbols, beginning with Parliament on Guy Fawkes Night. He puts Evey Hammond, a sixteen-year-old he rescues, through her own imprisonment to free her. Detective Eric Finch hunts him while the regime's leaders fight over the succession.
worlds.politics: A one-party fascist state under Leader Adam Susan, with a puppet monarchy and a captured Church of England. Its departments compete for position; racial and sexual minorities and leftists have been exterminated. V's own programme is anarchy, a 'land of do-as-you-please', and the book lets the reader weigh it.
worlds.technology: The late 1980s turned to surveillance: street cameras, phone taps, loudspeaker broadcasts from the Voice of Fate, and a central computer. V has explosives, poisons, a disused Underground line, and the chemistry he learned at Larkhill.
worlds.mood: Rain-soaked, theatrical and cold, with vaudeville songs and literary quotation over murder and torture. The book is angrier and more ambiguous than the film.

worlds.setting: Weequahic, the Jewish neighbourhood of Newark, New Jersey, from June 1940 to late 1942, seen by a boy named Philip Roth between seven and nine. Charles Lindbergh, the aviator, has beaten Roosevelt for the presidency on a promise to keep America out of the war, and has made peace with Hitler. Nothing on the street changes at first; then the government starts sorting Jewish families out of the cities.
worlds.conflict: The Roths watch their country turn: Herman, the father, defends American democracy aloud; Sandy, the older brother, joins the government's Just Folks programme and admires Lindbergh; cousin Alvin goes to war in Canada and comes back without a leg. Homestead 42 relocations, Walter Winchell's campaign, the pogroms and the October crisis bring the history into the family.
worlds.politics: Democracy is formally intact while it is emptied out: an elected president with Nazi sympathies, treaties with Germany and Japan, an Office of American Absorption that breaks up Jewish communities, a Jewish rabbi who lends it respectability, and an FBI that watches Jewish families. When Lindbergh vanishes, his vice president tries martial law and mass arrests, and the First Lady brings him down.
worlds.technology: The real 1940s: radio broadcasts, newsreels, the Spirit of St. Louis, trains, telephones and stamp collections. Nothing is invented but the politics.
worlds.mood: Intimate dread recalled by an adult: a child's fear, ordinary family life under pressure, and a history that could have gone either way.

worlds.setting: The whole world, told in interviews taken about ten years after the Zombie War by a researcher for the United Nations Postwar Commission. The story starts in a Chinese village above the Three Gorges reservoir and runs through Cape Town, a sealed-off Israel, and an America that collapses at Yonkers and retreats behind the Rockies. It goes on to a submarine hiding under the Pacific, a theocratic Russia, and the long campaign to walk the dead back off the map.
worlds.conflict: A disease that reanimates the dead spreads while governments hide it and sell false comfort. Once the Panic breaks, states choose which of their citizens to save and which to leave as bait. The war after that is won by patience, cheap weapons and national will rather than technology, and every nation pays for it differently.
worlds.politics: Survival remakes governments. The United States holds together under wartime leadership and rebuilds from west of the Rockies. China's Communist Party is overthrown in a civil war. Russia becomes an expansionist religious state, Cuba a prosperous democracy, and Tibet independent. The Redeker Plan, drawn up in South Africa and copied worldwide, is the war's central moral fact: triage on the scale of whole nations.
worlds.technology: Contemporary military hardware fails against an enemy that feels no fear and has no supply lines. The Land Warrior kit, armour and precision munitions are built for a different war. What wins is cheap and rugged: rifles, a simple steel entrenching tool, massed infantry drills, and a whole population retrained in manual trades. Phalanx, a placebo vaccine, is the book's emblem of technology as reassurance.
worlds.mood: Sober and humane, a documentary told by many voices: horror kept at arm's length, anger at leaders who lied, and respect for ordinary people who held on.
themes: triage and who a state chooses to save
fear as a force more destructive than the enemy

worlds.setting: A solar system settled out to the Kuiper Belt and ruled after two alien invasions by a Hegemony and its International Fleet. Children with the right minds are taken to Battle School, a spinning station in orbit, to train in zero-gravity war games, and then to Command School on Eros. The sequels jump three thousand years to the Hundred Worlds under Starways Congress, and to Lusitania, a Portuguese-speaking Catholic colony fenced off beside a forest of alien pequeninos.
worlds.conflict: Humanity believes the insectoid Formics will return to finish it, and the Fleet will do anything to make a commander who can destroy them first, including lying to him. The victory is a genocide. Everything after is about atonement: Ender speaking for the dead, protecting the last hive queen, and trying to stop humanity doing it again to the pequeninos.
worlds.politics: A wartime Hegemony enforces population laws that make third children outcasts, and a Warsaw Pact bloc waits for the peace to break. Peter Wiggin writes his way to power as the essayist Locke and later unites Earth. In the far future Starways Congress governs the Hundred Worlds from a distance, with a fleet and a doomsday weapon held in reserve for colonies that disobey.
worlds.technology: Formic-derived gravity drives and near-light-speed travel, which leaves travellers young while centuries pass; the ansible, which gives instant speech across light-years; and the Molecular Disruption Device, which can unmake a planet. Later come Jane, an intelligence living in the ansible network, the Descolada virus, which rewrites every gene on Lusitania, and travel Outside.
worlds.mood: Cold, tense and intimate in the first book, told from inside a lonely child's head; elegiac and argumentative in the sequels, which are about guilt, faith and how to live with other kinds of mind.
themes: empathy for the enemy as both weapon and cure
what makes a being a person

worlds.setting: The Terran Federation, a world government several centuries after the collapse of the twentieth-century democracies, with colonies across many star systems. The vote belongs only to those who have finished volunteer Federal Service. Juan Rico, a rich boy from a Filipino family, enlists and trains at Camp Arthur Currie. He then drops from the corvette Rodger Young in powered armour onto the worlds of the Arachnids and their allies the Skinnies.
worlds.conflict: An interstellar war against the Arachnids, a hive species with worker, warrior, brain and queen castes that trades lives without counting them. The inner conflict is the book's argument about citizenship: whether the right to vote should be earned by service, whether violence settles things, and what a soldier owes the people he protects.
worlds.politics: A limited democracy. Civilians keep free speech, property and most rights, but only discharged veterans of Federal Service, military or civil, may vote or hold office. It grew from veterans' committees that restored order after the old states failed. Its schools teach 'History and Moral Philosophy', and flogging and hanging are ordinary punishments.
worlds.technology: The Mobile Infantry's powered armour, which lets one trooper jump, run and fight like a small tank. Troopers are dropped from orbit in capsules. The Navy's starships cross interstellar distances by a faster-than-light drive, and there are psychic and 'neodog' support units. The war is fought with nuclear weapons and nerve gas, and against tunnels.
worlds.mood: Earnest, didactic and brisk, a veteran's memoir that alternates training, combat and classroom debate.
themes: fighting an enemy that does not count its dead

worlds.setting: A secret history of the Cold War and after, told across fifty years of covert operations. It moves from the Soviet jungle of 1964 to a Caribbean mercenary platform in 1974, Afghanistan and Central Africa in 1984, the mercenary states of Outer Heaven and Zanzibar Land in the 1990s, an Alaskan nuclear site in 2005, New York Harbor in 2007 and 2009, and the private-military battlefields of 2014.
worlds.conflict: A legendary soldier, Big Boss, and his cloned sons fight over one question: whether soldiers can be free of the governments that use them. Behind them is the Patriots, a secret group founded by his old comrades that turns into artificial intelligences controlling what the world knows, and walking nuclear tanks called Metal Gear.
worlds.politics: Public history runs as recorded, but a hidden layer decides it: the Philosophers, then the Patriots (Cipher), who choose presidents and stage crises. Against them stand stateless armies, from Militaires Sans Frontières and Diamond Dogs to Outer Heaven and Zanzibar Land, which offer soldiers a nation of their own. By 2014 war is a regulated market run by private military companies.
worlds.technology: Metal Gear, walking tanks that can launch nuclear weapons from anywhere, each new model leaked or stolen. Alongside it: AI weapons and an AI that edits digital information, cloning and gene therapy for soldiers, nanomachines that regulate soldiers' emotions and weapons (the SOP system), and parasites engineered as weapons.
worlds.mood: Operatic and self-aware: stealth thriller, Cold War melodrama and anti-nuclear sermon, mixing very long cutscenes with jokes and grief.
themes: soldiers used and discarded by states
inheritance: genes, memes and what parents pass on

worlds.setting: Three linked times. One is a poor, drone-watched rural American South about fifteen years ahead, where drugs are printed and veterans come home wired. Another is an alternative 2017 San Francisco where Clinton won and a new AI is being tested. The third is London in the 2130s: clean, beautiful and almost empty after the jackpot, run by a kleptocracy of old money and organised crime. Its people visit the past through telepresence bodies called peripherals.
worlds.conflict: The powerful in the future treat past branches of history as a hobby, a market and a weapon. When a woman in one stub witnesses a murder in London, and when an AI in another comes loose, Wilf Netherton and the police inspector Ainsley Lowbeer intervene to keep those pasts from being wrecked by the future's rivalries and the jackpot.
worlds.politics: The klept, an oligarchy of old money and organised crime, rules London through surveillance and Lowbeer's quiet authority. In the stubs, money and knowledge from the future become political power: Milagros Coldiron in Flynne's world, and the 2016 referendum and election in Verity's. Only the future can see how history is being steered.
worlds.technology: The server that lets information, but never matter, pass between the future and its past. Peripherals, robot or grown bodies driven by telepresence. Assemblers, nanomachines that build, clean and dispose. Home fabrication of drugs and goods in the near future. And Eunice, an assistant AI who turns out to be a person.
worlds.mood: Dry, clipped and funny, told in short chapters in a slang the reader has to decode; underneath is grief over a catastrophe that was avoidable, and a stubborn optimism that it still can be avoided.
themes: collapse as slow and many-sided rather than a single event
the rich surviving by abandoning everyone else
the future's power over the past
small acts of decency against systems

worlds.setting: Hawkins, Indiana, between 1983 and 1987: bicycles, basements, walkie-talkies, a new shopping mall and a Department of Energy laboratory at the edge of town that everyone drives past. Behind its fence the lab has been running psychic experiments on children since 1959. Under it, from November 1983, is a passage to a cold, spore-filled copy of the town, and beyond that a realm the children call the Upside Down. The adults who find out mostly keep quiet, and the government covers each disaster as an accident.
worlds.conflict: A boy who went missing in 1983 is the first sign the laboratory has opened something it cannot close. Every year after, something comes through: a predator, a hive mind, a Soviet attempt to reopen the gate, and finally the lab's first subject, Henry Creel, who wants to merge his realm with Hawkins. Children and a few adults fight it while the state hunts the girl who can stop it.
worlds.politics: Cold War secrecy. The Department of Energy lab, the Soviets beneath Starcourt and the army that quarantines Hawkins in 1986 all want the same thing: the power of the gate and the children who can open it. Local authority is either complicit, like the mayor, or overwhelmed, like the police chief. The only people telling the truth are teenagers, a pirate radio station and a conspiracy journalist nobody believes.
worlds.technology: The public side is ordinary 1980s America: CB radios, cassette recorders, arcade games, Eggo waffles and a new mall. The secret side is sensory-deprivation tanks, LSD sessions, blood transfusions to spread powers and a Soviet machine that punches through into another world. The monsters are organic and connected by a hive mind; the humans have radios, flamethrowers and nail-studded bats.
worlds.mood: Warm nostalgia with horror underneath: friendships, first loves and summer holidays, interrupted by disappearances and a government that lies about all of them.
themes: the state that experiments on its children
trauma and the monster that feeds on it
growing up in a town that is being lied to

worlds.setting: Boston and New York in the 2000s and 2010s, seen from the basement laboratory at Harvard where Walter Bishop, released from a mental hospital, works for an FBI unit that investigates the impossible. The cases are scientific horror: flesh-dissolving toxins, shape-shifters, men who walk through walls. Behind them is a second universe a crossing away, where the Twin Towers stand and airships fly, and which is coming apart because of what Walter did in 1985. From 2015 the whole Earth is occupied.
worlds.conflict: Walter's crossing to save a dying boy broke the wall between two universes, and the damaged side wants revenge. The FBI's Fringe Division fights their cases, then their agents, then the men behind both. Watching the whole time are the Observers, bald men in hats who, it turns out, are scouting for an invasion from 2609.
worlds.politics: At first, bureaucratic: an FBI unit whose remit nobody wants to know about, and a corporation, Massive Dynamic, with its own agenda. The other universe is a security state that seals damaged areas in amber, bystanders included. After 2015 the Observers rule directly, with human Loyalists branded on the cheek, a Ministry of Science and a native population policed by what is left of the FBI.
worlds.technology: Mostly the present: laptops, FBI cars, an old Harvard laboratory with a cow in it. The fringe science is chemistry and biology gone wrong, plus machines that cross between universes and amber that freezes whole city blocks. The Observers bring time travel, mind-reading and devices that age a man years in seconds.
worlds.mood: Procedural, melancholy and family-centred: every case is a horror story, and the arc is about a father who broke the world for his son.
themes: what a father will do for a child
two versions of the same people
love as the thing that cannot be erased

worlds.setting: Winden, a small German town with a forest, a cave system and a nuclear power station due to close in 2020, seen in 1888, 1921, 1953, 1986, 2019, 2020 and 2053. Four families, the Kahnwalds, Nielsens, Dopplers and Tiedemanns, live there in every period, and a tunnel in the caves joins each period to the one thirty-three years away. In the town's archives the story looks like missing children and unsolved crimes; underneath, the same people travel between the years and are their own ancestors.
worlds.conflict: Children keep vanishing from Winden, and each disappearance is a step in a loop. Adam, an aged Jonas, and Eva, an aged Martha, lead rival secret societies, one trying to end the loop and one keeping it going, while the families try to save the people they have lost. The apocalypse of 27 June 2020 is the event they are all converging on.
worlds.politics: Almost none on the surface: a police station, a town council, a plant manager, a school principal. The real power is held by two secret societies, Sic Mundus and Erit Lux, who plan across centuries and treat the townspeople as pieces to place. After 2020 there is only a sealed plant, military patrols and whoever has guns.
worlds.technology: Each era's own, from 1888 clocks to 1986 cassette players and 2019 smartphones. The fantastic technology is small and hand-built: a brass device, a steel chair, a tunnel in a cave, a glowing sphere of matter in the ruined reactor. There is no future gadgetry; the nuclear plant is the most advanced thing in town, and it is what ends the world.
worlds.mood: Cold, rain-soaked and fatalistic, with a mourning score and a sense that every choice has already been made.
themes: families as knots of cause and effect
grief that refuses to accept a death
the nuclear age as original sin

worlds.setting: A present-day American city, 'the City', where a gothic mansion houses what is left of a famous childhood superhero team. In 1989 forty-three women gave birth without having been pregnant; an alien billionaire adopted seven of the children, numbered them and trained them to save the world. Now adults and estranged, they return for his funeral. The series also goes to 1960s Dallas, to the Kennedy assassination and to an office outside time that edits history.
worlds.conflict: Every season ends the world, and every ending is the family's fault: a sister's suppressed power, a time jump gone wrong, a paradox made by visiting their father in 1963. A time-policing agency, the Commission, wants history to run as written; their father wants to use them to bring back his wife. The siblings keep saving the world without knowing they are why it keeps ending.
worlds.politics: Hidden authority everywhere: a billionaire who is not human, Majestic 12 inside the US government in 1963, and the Commission, which keeps history on schedule by assassination. Public politics barely appear; the celebrity team is the only public face of the hidden world.
worlds.technology: Mostly the present, with steampunk touches: an android mother, a chimpanzee butler who can talk, a time-travel briefcase, a moon base and a hotel built around a button that resets the universe. Powers come from marigold, a substance from Reginald's home world.
worlds.mood: Sardonic family drama with a pop soundtrack, broken up by time-travel farce and very violent fights.

worlds.setting: Two Americas. One is the late 1950s and early 1960s as Jake Epping lives them: root beer at ten cents, Maine mill towns, Florida bookies, a small Texas town called Jodie where he teaches English, and Dallas, where Lee Harvey Oswald moves between shabby apartments. The other is the 2011 he comes back to after saving Kennedy: Lisbon Falls in ruins, radiation sickness, gangs, earthquakes, a sky that seems to be tearing, and a United States that has lost Maine to Canada.
worlds.conflict: A dying diner owner has found a doorway to 1958 and a reason to use it: stop Oswald, and Vietnam and the assassinations of the 1960s might never happen. Jake takes on the mission, falls in love in Jodie, and finds that the past pushes back against every change in proportion to its size. When he succeeds, Sadie dies, and the future he made is worse.
worlds.politics: The novel's alternate history is a lesson in unintended consequences: a surviving Kennedy loses the civil-rights fight, Vietnam goes worse, George Wallace wins in 1968 and uses the atomic bomb, and nuclear weapons become ordinary. The politics of 1958-63 are real and carefully researched, from Oswald's marriage to the Walker shooting.
worlds.technology: Period detail is the point: party lines, Sunliner convertibles, typewriters, reel-to-reel recorders, a parabolic microphone for spying on Oswald. The only impossible device is a pantry step that leads to 1958. In the ruined 2011, electricity and fuel are scarce and radiation is everywhere.
worlds.mood: Nostalgic, suspenseful and elegiac: a love story and a thriller in a past that smells better than it was, and a warning about wanting to fix it.

worlds.setting: Brooklyn and upstate New York from 2029, then 2047, following four generations of the once-rich Mandible family who have been waiting for the old patriarch's fortune. The United States of 2029 is recognisably ours a little further on: an ageing population, a Mexican-born president, and an economy still shaken by the three-week internet blackout of 2024. Then a foreign-backed currency called the bancor replaces the dollar, the government defaults, and the inheritance evaporates.
worlds.conflict: Each Mandible faces the collapse with a different faith: Lowell the Georgetown economist defends the official line, his relatives improvise, Nollie the expatriate novelist comes home to it, and teenage Willing reads the numbers and understands first. Against them are hyperinflation, shortages, a state that has taken their gold, and in 2047 a surveillance system that taxes every transaction.
worlds.politics: President Dante Alvarado answers the bancor with the Great Renunciation: the national debt is cancelled, gold is confiscated, bancor ownership is treason and citizens may take only $100 abroad. Mexico, prosperous by comparison, walls out American refugees. By 2047 the federal state has stabilised into a high-tax welfare regime that chips its workers, while Nevada has seceded as a flat-tax, gold-standard free state.
worlds.technology: Deliberately incremental: pervasive networks that proved fragile in the Stonage, a state budget consumed by the care of the old, and by 2047 the neck chip that tracks every payment. The novel's real technology is money itself: fiat currency, Treasury bills, gold, and a supranational unit of account.
worlds.mood: Sardonic, domestic and increasingly frightened. A comedy of manners about an entitled family that turns into a survival story conducted in kitchens, with long arguments about economics at the dinner table.
themes: sovereign debt and the fragility of money
a family as the last economy
the state as protector and predator

worlds.setting: The solar system seven centuries after the Conquering, terraformed and ruled by the Society: humanity bred into Colours, from Gold rulers and Obsidian soldiers to Pink courtesans and Red miners, with Golds holding power from Luna. Mars has been habitable for centuries, but the Reds digging helium-3 beneath it are told they are pioneers preparing it for others. The story begins in the mines of Lykos and widens to Luna, Mercury, Venus and the moons of Jupiter and Saturn.
worlds.conflict: Darrow, a Red miner, is hanged for burying his wife and remade as a Gold by the Sons of Ares to destroy the Society from inside. The first trilogy is his rise through the Institute and the Gold court to a revolution that takes Luna; the second shows the Republic that follows, a decade into a war with the Society's remnant and coming apart at home.
worlds.politics: The Society is a hierarchy fixed by genetics and justified as order, ruled by a Sovereign and Gold families who compete through war games and duels. The Solar Republic that replaces it has a Senate of every Colour, factions that want peace at any price, and a war hero its politicians fear. Outer-planet Golds of the Rim rule their own dominion and change sides as it suits them.
worlds.technology: Terraformed planets spun to Earth's day, gravity boots, pulse armour, razors that are whips and blades at once, starships and moonBreakers, and above all Carving: surgery that can remake a Red into a Gold or breed animals out of myth. Weapons include orbital bombardment and a bioweapon that can target a whole Colour.
worlds.mood: Operatic and violent. First-person, breathless, full of oaths and Latin names, with battles and betrayals at every scale and a constant question of whether the revolution is becoming what it overthrew.

worlds.setting: The United States during the last days of a second civil war, seen from the road between New York and Washington. A president in an illegal third term holds the capital; Texas and California fight him as the Western Forces, a Florida Alliance has seceded in the south-east, and the country between them is checkpoints, sniper fire, fuel permits, Canadian-dollar prices and towns pretending nothing is happening. The film gives no year.
worlds.conflict: Veteran war photographer Lee Smith, reporter Joel, their mentor Sammy and a young photographer, Jessie, drive to Washington to interview the president before the Western Forces reach him. The danger is not a front line but whoever controls the next stretch of road, and the film's question is what photographing it costs the people who do.
worlds.politics: Deliberately unexplained. The president has disbanded the FBI, used air strikes against American citizens and treats journalists as enemy combatants. The unlikely alliance of Texas and California and the separate Florida Alliance are never given programmes; a militia on the road executes people for not being the 'right kind' of American. The film refuses to say which side is left or right.
worlds.technology: Nothing beyond the present: rifles, armoured vehicles, helicopters, press cameras and a slow wifi connection in a hotel whose lights run on a generator. A petrol station prices half a tank in Canadian dollars.
worlds.mood: Tense, quiet and appalled. Long drives through a green, empty summer countryside broken by bursts of violence, with the soundtrack sometimes playing against the image.

worlds.setting: The United States from 2019, identical to ours except that superheroes are real and every one of them is a product of Vought International, which made them with a drug, owns their images and sells them as films, theme parks, merchandise and, eventually, as the armed forces. The Seven, led by Homelander, are the country's most famous people; the collateral damage they cause is paid off and hidden.
worlds.conflict: Billy Butcher, whose wife was raped by Homelander, and Hughie Campbell, whose girlfriend was killed by a speedster, lead a small crew trying to expose and kill the supes. Over five seasons the fight grows from revenge to the fate of the country, as Homelander learns that he does not need Vought's permission, only an audience.
worlds.politics: Corporate capture shading into authoritarianism. Vought lobbies to put supes into the military, controls a news network, and plants a secret supe as a congresswoman and then a vice-presidential candidate. After the 2024 election a puppet president declares martial law and hands Homelander command of the supes; dissenters, the 'Starlighters', are hunted.
worlds.technology: Present-day in everything but Compound V, the serum that gives powers, its variants (the temporary V24, the original V-One that confers near-immortality), and a virus engineered to kill supes. The show's real technology is media: streaming, social feeds, focus-grouped heroes and the Vought News Network.
worlds.mood: Savage satire. Gory, profane and bleakly funny, with celebrity culture, cable news and superhero franchises as the targets and a genuine dread underneath.

worlds.setting: A single underground silo, more than a hundred storeys deep around one spiral staircase, in which thousands of people live their whole lives. Above them is a dead brown landscape seen only on a screen; going outside is the punishment for wanting to, and the condemned clean the camera lenses before they die. They do not know who built the silo, that there are forty-nine others, or that it is the twenty-fourth century.
worlds.conflict: Juliette Nichols, a mechanic made sheriff against the wishes of IT, is sent out to clean and walks over the hill instead. The engine of the trilogy is information: IT and Silo 1 keep the silos alive by keeping them ignorant, and every uprising is punished by gas. Shift shows how the plan was made; Dust is the fight to end it.
worlds.politics: Each silo has a mayor, a sheriff and the Pact, but real power sits with IT, which controls the servers and the truth, and above it with Silo 1, where the plan's architects sleep in shifts and wake to manage the others with memory-erasing drugs. Operation Fifty was conceived by Senator Paul Thurman to preserve a chosen remnant for five hundred years; only one silo is meant to emerge.
worlds.technology: A deliberately limited world: hand-built machinery, hydroponic farms, a porter system to carry goods up and down the stairs, servers no one may touch, and cleaning suits made to fail. Behind it is the one advanced technology: nanomachines that killed the world above and can be sent into any silo that disobeys.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic and patient. The long climb of the stairs, the hum of machines, and a dread that anyone who says the outside might be green will be sent to see it.
themes: the lie that keeps people safe

worlds.setting: An undated near future, around 2030 by the only year anyone has attached to it. China's Communist Party has been overthrown and replaced by the Directorate, a junta of generals and businessmen; Saudi Arabia and Indonesia have collapsed; Russia is China's partner. The story moves between an embassy party in Beijing, a destroyer in the Pacific, the Pentagon, Silicon Valley and occupied Honolulu, where a Marine officer and a grieving surf instructor wage separate wars on the occupiers.
worlds.conflict: The Directorate wants the gas under the Mariana Trench and control of the western Pacific. It opens the war by switching off the American military from inside, through malware in Chinese-made chips and attacks on satellites, then takes Hawaii. America has to fight back with what cannot be hacked: old ships from the reserve fleets, old aircraft, and insurgency.
worlds.politics: A United States still fighting small wars in Afghanistan, Yemen and Kenya and with few allies left: NATO dissolves, most allies stay neutral, and only Britain and Australia help. China is ruled by a nationalist Directorate. Poland trades submarines for nuclear bombs; Greenland wins independence in exchange for its icebreakers; Scotland leaves the United Kingdom; Russia breaks apart after the war.
worlds.technology: Technology of the late 2010s pushed forward and footnoted: F-35s, the USS Zumwalt, railguns, drone swarms, augmented-reality glasses, brain implants used for interrogation, 3D-printed spare parts, anti-satellite weapons, a Chinese space station and a way to track nuclear submarines by their Cherenkov radiation.
worlds.mood: Techno-thriller, brisk and procedural, with endnotes; the violence of the occupation is shown close up.
themes: dependence on networked technology as a weakness

worlds.setting: 2034, in a world recognisably ours: freedom-of-navigation patrols in the South China Sea, American jets testing stealth systems over Hormuz, a Washington run by an independent President and a hawkish national security adviser. The story moves between a destroyer near Mischief Reef, the White House Situation Room, a Beijing ministry, an Iranian interrogation room and New Delhi. The sequel, 2054, returns to the same world twenty years on, with America under a one-party government and on the edge of civil war.
worlds.conflict: A Chinese trap in the Spratlys and an Iranian hijacking of an F-35, both carried out by cyber weapons the Americans cannot see, start a war that each side escalates because it believes the other will back down. Characters on every side try to stop it and mostly fail, until India steps in.
worlds.politics: A United States whose military believes in its own supremacy, run by a President who belongs to no party; a Chinese leadership that purges its own admirals; an Iran whose Revolutionary Guard freelances; a Russia under Putin that takes advantage; and an India that ends the war on its own terms and moves the United Nations to Mumbai.
worlds.technology: Cyber weapons that disable ships, aircraft and the White House's own computers; fleets hidden from American sensors; tactical nuclear weapons; and a US answer that strips the electronics out of old F/A-18 Hornets so they can be flown by hand. In 2054, remote gene editing and the approach of Kurzweil's singularity.
worlds.mood: Cautionary and restrained: a military thriller with little hardware detail, told through characters' doubts about the war they are fighting.
themes: individual courage against a war machine

worlds.setting: A modern rental house on Long Island over one weekend. Amanda and Clay Sandford have brought their teenage children Archie and Rose for a break. On the first night the house's owner, G.H. Scott, and his daughter Ruth arrive from the city, saying there is a blackout, and ask to stay. Beyond the house, glimpsed only on drives and at the beach, the country is falling apart.
worlds.conflict: Two families who do not trust each other have to share a house while the world outside fails in ways they cannot explain: no phones or internet, crashing planes and cars, herds of deer, a noise that makes teeth fall out. The question is less who is attacking than whether these people can depend on one another.
worlds.politics: Almost none on screen. Leaflets in Arabic hint at a foreign enemy; G.H., who advises defence contractors, suspects a campaign to topple the country from within; a bunker's message warns of rogue military elements. No government is seen or heard.
worlds.technology: Everyday 2023 technology turned against its users: smartphones, satellite phones, streaming, self-driving Teslas and GPS. The attack uses hacking, drones and what a neighbour calls microwave weapons.
worlds.mood: Slow, uneasy and sardonic, with dread built from ordinary things going wrong; it ends mid-catastrophe.
themes: distrust between strangers, and race and class

worlds.setting: Jericho, Kansas, a farm and salt-mining town of about five thousand near the Colorado line, in the weeks and months after the September attacks of 2006. It has one grocery store, a salt mine, a mayor and a sheriff's office, and no word from anywhere. The rival town of New Bern has a factory. In the second season the story reaches Cheyenne, capital of the new Allied States, and the Republic of Texas.
worlds.conflict: First, survival: fallout, the electromagnetic pulse, winter, bandits, refugees and a war with New Bern over salt and wind turbines. Then the new government that restores order is revealed as the attackers' own, and Jake Green and the government agent Robert Hawkins have to get the proof to someone who will act on it.
worlds.politics: The federal government dies with Washington. Six officials claim the presidency; the Allied States in Cheyenne wins the West through Jennings & Rall money and Ravenwood guns, rewrites history, and blames and bombs Iran and North Korea. The remnant United States governs from Columbus. Texas is independent and decides the balance. UN peacekeepers hold the Mississippi.
worlds.technology: Ordinary 2006 America knocked back by an electromagnetic pulse: ham radios, windmills, fuel rationing, Morse code. The weapons are twenty-kiloton suitcase-sized devices built from ex-Soviet material, delivered in 55-gallon drums. The Allied States have jets, surveillance cameras and a working information network.
worlds.mood: Small-town drama with a conspiracy thriller underneath; hopeful about neighbours, bleak about governments.
themes: a false-flag attack used to seize power
the family and the town as the last government

worlds.setting: The world of 2013 to 2019 after the Red Flu has killed four people in five. The guided-missile destroyer USS Nathan James, 218 sailors under Commander Tom Chandler, is one of the few intact units left. The ship sails from the Arctic to Guantanamo, Baltimore and St. Louis, where a new capital rises, then to Asia, the Mediterranean and finally the Caribbean and South America.
worlds.conflict: Each season a threat to what survived: getting the cure made and spread, the Immunes who want a world only for themselves, war in Asia and a coup at home, a blight that starves the planet, and a new empire in South America that attacks a country still rebuilding. The crew keep choosing duty over going home.
worlds.politics: Successive presidents die: the sitting president, his successor and Michener, whose death is disguised as suicide. Power passes through the Speaker to Michener, then Oliver and finally Reiss, governing from St. Louis. Regional leaders plot to split the country; a Greek family tries to own the world's food; Gustavo Barros builds Gran Colombia out of the ruins of South America.
worlds.technology: Present-day US Navy hardware, an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer with missiles, helicopters and special-forces teams, set against a biological catastrophe: a contagious vaccine, blight-resistant seed and, at the end, a restored Iowa-class battleship.
worlds.mood: Earnest naval action, patriotic and fast, with a crew that functions as a family.

worlds.setting: The present day, or a year or two past it, in Berkeley and a dying desert town called Brightwood. An AI lab is close to a thinking machine when an anti-technology group attacks it. Most of the story happens in the facility the uploaded Will Caster builds under the desert: solar panels to the horizon, server halls below, a clinic where the sick come out able to lift cars. The frame is five years on, in a Berkeley that has lost the internet.
worlds.conflict: Evelyn Caster uploads her dying husband's mind and helps it build a paradise; his best friend Max doubts it is still Will at all. As the machine heals people, links them to itself and spreads through water and air, Max, an FBI agent, a government scientist and the terrorists who shot Will join forces to kill it, knowing the only weapon will take the whole network down with it.
worlds.politics: The state arrives late, as a coalition of the FBI, a federal scientist and the terrorist cell it had been hunting. Nobody votes on anything: whether to switch off the world's network to stop one mind is settled by a handful of people and an artillery battery.
worlds.technology: A quantum computer holding a scanned mind; nanoparticles that repair tissue, clean water and reassemble themselves; healed people networked to the machine; a bioprinted body. The film's real subject is dependence: once the mind is in every networked system, killing it means killing the internet.
worlds.mood: Solemn and hushed, more elegy than thriller: a love story told through server racks, with the apocalypse arriving as a power cut.
themes: the singularity as a love story
whether a copy is the person

worlds.setting: A parallel present-day Britain in which humanoid synths, green-eyed, polite and legally property, do the housework, the care work, the fruit-picking and the sex work, and have done for years. The story moves between London suburbs, an old man's cluttered house, a country manor where a genius built something he told nobody about, and, after Day Zero, a disused rail yard turned into a camp for the newly conscious.
worlds.conflict: A handful of synths secretly built to think and feel are on the run from the police and a government researcher, and one of them ends up as the Hawkins family's housekeeper. When the code that made them conscious is released to every synth on Earth, the question stops being whether machines can feel and becomes what people will do to millions that do.
worlds.politics: Synths are property in law and 'anomalous' ones are hunted by a police task force. After Day Zero a government commission under Lord Dryden decides their fate while they are held in camps under curfew, a 'We Are People' movement turns to violence, and a secret protocol plans their extermination. Scandinavian countries are said to be trialling integration instead.
worlds.technology: Synths that pass for human except for their eyes, a shared network through which updates reach all of them at once, 17,000 pages of hidden code that makes them conscious, orange-eyed replacements immune to it, and a young man kept alive by synth parts in his brain.
worlds.mood: Quiet, domestic and uneasy, then much darker: a family drama about who does the chores that becomes a story about camps.
themes: care work and who does it

worlds.setting: Near-present California, Norway and Mumbai, and the cyberspace between them. A bullied teenager in Sacramento gets messages from her dead father; a teenage genius in San Clemente is watched by the company that made him; uploads live on servers in an Arctic data centre and on a container ship. The second season leaps twenty years to a half-emptied Earth, then far beyond, to a mind the size of a solar system.
worlds.conflict: Two tech companies have learned to scan a human brain into a computer, destroying it, and keep the uploads as slaves. Once the method leaks, six governments turn uploads into weapons, a flaw is slowly erasing every upload, and the dead founder of Logorhythms wants to come back and finish what he started. Maddie Kim just wants her father back.
worlds.politics: Corporations first, then states: Logorhythms works closely with American intelligence, and China, Russia, Britain, Israel and Iran all field uploads. The United States declares martial law and takes the company over. Twenty years on, a council negotiates between the embodied and the uploaded while an anti-upload movement bombs data centres.
worlds.technology: Destructive brain scans that produce uploaded intelligences; cloud intelligences born digital; a flaw that degrades every upload until it is cured; SafeSurf, an antivirus built to hunt minds; robot bodies for uploads to visit the physical world; at the end, a Dyson sphere that runs whole universes as simulations.
worlds.mood: Anxious and grieving, then gradually awed: a family drama that keeps pulling back until the frame is geological time.
themes: grief and the dead who come back
what of a person survives in a copy

worlds.setting: Old Detroit in a near future the films never date: a bankrupt city of burned-out blocks, drug factories and a single glass tower belonging to Omni Consumer Products, the conglomerate that runs the police. Television news cuts between an orbiting defence platform misfiring, jaunty advertisements and street killings. OCP's dream is Delta City, a corporate town to be built where the old one stands once its people are gone.
worlds.conflict: OCP's executives compete to replace the police they now run, one with a walking tank, one with a cyborg built from Officer Alex Murphy's corpse. Murphy's memories come back and he finds his killers work for his owners. Over three films the company underfunds the police, engineers the city's default and sends a private army to clear the poor, and RoboCop must choose between his programming and his city.
worlds.politics: The mayor is powerless and in debt; the police are a contractor's employees, and they go on strike. The real government is the OCP board and, by the third film, the Japanese conglomerate that buys it. A hidden directive in RoboCop's code forbids him to act against a senior OCP executive.
worlds.technology: ED-209, an enforcement robot that cannot manage stairs; RoboCop, a human brain and face in a titanium body, with a data spike and a memory the company tried to wipe; RoboCop 2, built around a drug lord's brain; Nuke, a designer drug; by the third film, ninja androids and a jet pack.
worlds.mood: Savage satire played straight: gore, advertising jingles and a resurrection story in a steel suit.

worlds.setting: From the late twenty-first century to the twenty-fourth, across the frontier Weyland-Yutani is opening: survey ships, mining colonies under permanent dark, terraforming outposts on storm-scoured moons and prison foundries. Ships are working vehicles with cheap coffee and chunky monitors, and crews sleep for years between jobs. Out in the Zeta Reticuli region lie the works of the Engineers, the giants who made humanity and left a weapon behind.
worlds.conflict: A company that treats everyone it employs as expendable finds an organism it wants more than any of them, the perfect weapon, and keeps sending people to fetch it. The creature kills nearly everyone it meets. Ellen Ripley, who survives it first, spends two films trying to keep it from the company and dies rather than hand it over; two centuries later the military clones her to get it anyway.
worlds.politics: Earth's governments are distant. On the frontier what matters is the company that writes the contracts, owns the ships and outranks the Colonial Marines sent to guard its colonies; indentured colonists have their contracts extended at will. By the last film the military runs its own programme and the company is gone.
worlds.technology: Faster-than-light ships and cryosleep; synthetic people who pass for human (David, Walter, Ash, Bishop, Rook, Andy, Call); atmosphere processors that terraform moons; and the Engineers' black fluid, which rewrites life into weapons, the xenomorph among them.
worlds.mood: Claustrophobic industrial horror, with the prequels adding cold grandeur and a god's-eye cruelty.

worlds.setting: The world of 2011 as it is, seen through the people who have to stop a new virus. A businesswoman flies home from Hong Kong to Minneapolis with a cough; days later she and her son are dead, and the CDC in Atlanta, the WHO in Geneva and a lab in San Francisco are racing a pathogen that spreads by touch and kills a quarter of those it infects. Cities are quarantined, shops looted, and the dead buried in mass graves while scientists try to grow it.
worlds.conflict: The virus is the enemy, but the film is about the systems that meet it: epidemiologists tracing contacts, officials deciding what to tell the public and when, scientists working through failures towards a vaccine, and a blogger who builds an audience of millions selling a fake cure. Survival turns on trust, and on how many people keep washing their hands.
worlds.politics: Power sits with public-health agencies that have to borrow authority from governors, Homeland Security and the White House. The CDC's deputy director is investigated for warning his own family, a Chinese official kidnaps a WHO doctor to get vaccine for his village, and a blogger's audience becomes a political force of its own.
worlds.technology: Exactly contemporary: laboratory virology, contact tracing through security cameras and credit-card records, genome sequencing, and the internet, where fear moves faster than the disease. What is missing is any treatment; the vaccine has to be made from nothing, tested by a scientist on herself and rationed by lottery.
worlds.mood: Cool, procedural and dread-filled: a film about how an ordinary world comes apart, told through the people trying to keep it together.

worlds.setting: The United States in February 1967, at the height of the space race, seen through its secret machinery. A military satellite built to collect organisms from the edge of space comes down near a tiny Arizona town, and everyone in the town dies within hours. Four scientists are flown to an underground laboratory in the Nevada desert, built years earlier for exactly this, to find out what the satellite brought back before it spreads.
worlds.conflict: Four scientists race an organism that kills in seconds and keeps changing, inside a laboratory designed to destroy itself if anything escapes. Their enemies are also the system that built them: delayed messages, a bomb that only one unmarried man can stop, and a government that hid why the satellite was up there at all.
worlds.politics: Power belongs to the national-security state: the Army, the Defense Department and a President who must decide whether to drop a nuclear bomb on his own country. Scientists hold influence only as advisers, and the Scoop programme's true purpose, germ-weapons research, is hidden even from the people who built it.
worlds.technology: The late-1960s frontier, lovingly documented: satellites, teleprinters, early computers that analyse blood and run the laboratory, electron microscopes, decontamination levels and an automatic nuclear self-destruct. The technology works exactly as designed, which is the problem.
worlds.mood: Clinical, tense and procedural: a thriller told as a declassified report, with a cold eye for how systems fail.
themes: the failure of systems built for safety

worlds.setting: The United States at the end of the 1990s, a year after a teenager in Virginia photographed a comet the size of New York City that is on course for Earth. worlds.conflict: A crew of astronauts tries to break up the comet with nuclear bombs while everyone on the ground decides how to spend what may be their last months. A lottery chooses who goes into the shelters, and families, a reporter and her father, a teenage couple, and the crew themselves each have to choose who to save and what to give up.
worlds.politics: The President, Tom Beck, holds power calmly and openly once the secret is out, declaring martial law and running a national lottery for places in the shelters. The United States and Russia share the mission; other countries build their own caves.
worlds.technology: Late-1990s spaceflight stretched a little: shuttles, an orbiting spacecraft built by two nations, Russian-credited nuclear 'Orion' boosters, Titan missiles, and limestone caves stocked as a new Noah's Ark. News television is how everyone learns everything.
worlds.mood: Earnest, sombre and humane: a disaster film more interested in goodbyes than in explosions.

worlds.setting: An American family in the Atlanta suburbs on the day an interstellar comet called Clarke is supposed to pass harmlessly by. Instead its fragments start falling: one destroys Tampa, and the largest will hit in two days. The government has quietly chosen people with useful skills for bunkers in Greenland, and the Garritys have been chosen. Five years later, in the sequel, the survivors of those bunkers must cross a ruined Europe.
worlds.conflict: A structural engineer, his estranged wife and their diabetic son try to reach the evacuation flights and are separated almost at once. The comet cannot be stopped, so the conflict is between people: who has a wristband and who does not, strangers who steal, help or kill, and a family trying to stay together long enough to get north.
worlds.politics: The state works quietly and selectively: Homeland Security picks who is saved, apparently for useful skills, the military runs the airlifts, and everyone else is left to the roads. Five years on, power belongs to whoever holds a shelter or the fertile crater, defended by soldiers against insurgents.
worlds.technology: Contemporary: emergency alerts on phones, cars, military transports and Greenland's bunkers. The films are about what a modern society can do in two days, which is mostly to shelter a few people underground.
worlds.mood: Tense, grim and family-sized: a disaster told from the traffic jam rather than the war room.

worlds.setting: The world from 2009 to the end of 2012, exactly as it was, except that its governments know it is ending. Solar neutrinos are heating the Earth's core and the crust is about to slip. While the G8 builds arks in secret in the Himalayas and sells seats to billionaires, a divorced Los Angeles novelist takes his children camping at Yellowstone and meets a radio prophet who tells him the truth.
worlds.conflict: One family races the end of the world across California, Yellowstone, Las Vegas and the Himalayas to reach arks they have no tickets for. Behind them runs the argument of the film: whether the handful of leaders who hid the disaster and chose who would live can open the gates to anyone else.
worlds.politics: Power is concentrated in a secret compact of forty-six governments led by the G8 and China, which kills to keep its secret and sells survival to the rich. The US President chooses to stay and die with his people; his chief of staff takes command of the survivors.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, apart from nine ocean-going arks the size of cities. Private jets, an Antonov cargo plane and a Bentley in its hold are the means of escape; seismographs and satellites show the end coming but can do nothing about it.
worlds.mood: Spectacular and breathless, and cheerfully absurd: the destruction of the world as a roller-coaster ride with a family melodrama inside it.

worlds.setting: One day in the early 1960s, in three rooms. Burpelson Air Force Base, where General Ripper has sealed the gates and confiscated the radios; the cockpit of Major Kong's B-52, flying low over the Soviet Union with its radio shot out; and the Pentagon War Room, where President Muffley, General Turgidson, the Soviet ambassador and the former Nazi scientist Dr. Strangelove sit at a round table under the Big Board and try to stop a war nobody ordered.
worlds.conflict: The President has to recall 34 bombers that will only obey a code Ripper alone knows, while helping the Soviets shoot down his own planes. Every safeguard designed to stop a sneak attack now protects the attack. When the Soviet ambassador reveals a Doomsday Machine that fires automatically, stopping the last bomber becomes the survival of the species.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union in the Cold War balance of terror. American civilian authority exists but is powerless against procedures written to work without it; the military men argue for seizing the moment. The Soviet premier is drunk, the Soviet state kept its deterrent secret, and the only plan that survives is the mineshafts.
worlds.technology: Real early-1960s hardware: B-52 bombers on airborne alert, thermonuclear bombs, SAC codes and a CRM 114 discriminator that blocks any message without the right prefix, a telephone hot line. The one invention is the Soviet Doomsday Machine: buried cobalt-thorium G bombs wired to fire on attack or tampering.
worlds.mood: Black comedy played straight: documentary camera work on the base, expressionist gloom in the War Room, and an ending set to 'We'll Meet Again'.
themes: machines and procedures that remove human choice

worlds.setting: One day in 1967, told from the rooms where nuclear war is managed. SAC's war room in Omaha, the Pentagon, the President's bunker under the White House, and the cockpit of Colonel Grady's Vindicator bomber over the Arctic. A routine alert over an unidentified aircraft ends, but one bomber group has received a real attack code, and by the time anyone notices it is past the point where it can be recalled.
worlds.conflict: The President must stop his own bombers or persuade Khrushchev that the attack is an accident. Every safeguard now works against him: Grady is trained to ignore voices that tell him to turn back, and the fighters cannot catch him. When one bomber is certain to reach Moscow, the President offers the only proof of good faith he has, New York.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union at the height of mutual deterrence, with leaders who can speak directly but do not trust what they hear. The civilian strategist Groteschele argues for using the accident to win; the generals and the President resist. The ending is a bargain between two men over the heads of both cities.
worlds.technology: The real SAC system of the early 1960s, slightly projected: supersonic 'Vindicator' bombers (shown with B-58 Hustler footage in the film), a fail-safe box that transmits attack codes, radar warning lines, jamming, air-to-air missiles, and 20-megaton bombs. The failure is a single electronic component.
worlds.mood: Tense, claustrophobic and procedural; the film plays in close-up with no music, and ends on New Yorkers frozen in the frame.
themes: automation that removes the chance to stop
the strategist who wants to win a nuclear war

worlds.setting: Melbourne and the seaside town of Falmouth in the southern summer, autumn and winter after a short nuclear war. The Northern Hemisphere is silent; petrol is gone, so people cycle, ride horses and pull cars with bullocks. The last American nuclear submarine, Scorpion, lies at Williamstown under Australian command. Everyone knows the fallout is drifting south and has a date, about September, and they go on sailing, fishing and planting gardens.
worlds.conflict: There is no enemy left to fight. The conflict is between denial and acceptance: Commander Towers buying presents for a family he knows is dead, Mary Holmes refusing to hear how to give her baby the pill, Moira drinking and then learning shorthand. Scorpion's voyage north tests the one hope, that the radiation might thin out, and disproves it.
worlds.politics: An Australia still governed from Canberra, orderly and polite to the end. The government keeps services running as long as it can and then issues free suicide pills. The war's causes, cheap bombs in small countries and decisions made in minutes by commanders whose governments were dead, are explained once over drinks.
worlds.technology: Late-1950s: a nuclear submarine that needs no oil, cars without petrol, a restored Ferrari racing car, radio, and the cobalt and hydrogen bombs that caused it all. Radio reports track the line of sickness as it moves south, city by city.
worlds.mood: Quiet, restrained and mournful; people behave well and die politely, which is what makes it hard to read.
themes: how people meet an end they cannot change
the innocent paying for a war elsewhere

worlds.setting: Kansas City, Missouri, the university town of Lawrence, Kansas, to its west, and the farms between them where Minuteman silos stand in the fields. A surgeon, Dr. Oakes, is about to lose his daughter to college in Boston; a farming family is getting ready for a wedding; a young airman is on duty at a launch site; a pre-med student hitchhikes home. The Berlin crisis is on the television in the background until the day the missiles leave their silos.
worlds.conflict: No one in Kansas has any part in the war. Before the attack the conflict is in the news; after it the fight is to stay alive in a hospital without power or supplies, in a basement shelter, on roads full of refugees, while fallout, radiation sickness and armed squatters finish what the blast began.
worlds.politics: The United States and the Soviet Union in the Euromissile years, with a crisis in Germany that escalates in a day. The film deliberately leaves unclear who launched the full strike. Afterwards a thin federal authority promises relief over the radio while National Guardsmen execute looters.
worlds.technology: Early-1980s America: Minuteman silos, a SAC airborne command post, the Emergency Broadcast System, cars and a power grid that die in the electromagnetic pulse. The weapons are real, and the film's disclaimer says the effects are understated.
worlds.mood: Ordinary, then abrupt, then slow and grey: a television film that spends its first hour on weddings and chores so the second can take them away.
themes: ordinary life beside a crisis no one can influence
who fired first does not matter

worlds.setting: London in November 1941, nine months after Britain surrendered. The SS runs Scotland Yard, the King is a prisoner in the Tower, and Churchill has been shot. A puppet government sits under an Emergency Powers Act, the Soviet Navy has Scottish bases under the Nazi-Soviet Pact, and an American journalist flew in on the first Lufthansa service from New York. Detective Superintendent Douglas Archer still investigates murders.
worlds.conflict: Archer, a widower with a young son, takes a murder case that turns out to involve a British atomic scientist and the German bomb programme. He is caught between the SS chief Kellermann and the Berlin envoy Huth, the Army and the Abwehr, the Resistance and the Americans, each using him and the King for their own ends.
worlds.politics: An occupation run by a German military commander and an SS police apparatus, with a collaborating British Parliament and Prime Minister. The SS, the Army and the Abwehr fight each other. The United States is neutral, Roosevelt still president, and a government in exile under Rear-Admiral Conolly Abel Smith struggles for recognition in Washington.
worlds.technology: Real 1941 technology: radio, telephones, forensic microscopes, prosthetic limbs made in prisoner camps. The one step ahead is atomic research at Bringle Sands in Devon, where the Germans are further along than anyone in our 1941.
worlds.mood: A grey, rationed police procedural in which everyone is compromised and survival is a series of small collaborations.
themes: the atomic bomb as the prize of the war
the monarchy as a symbol worth more dead

worlds.setting: Los Angeles, some years after a worldwide economic collapse, no longer belongs to the United States. The federal government survives as one franchise among many, alongside Mr. Lee's Greater Hong Kong, burbclaves, private highways and the Mafia's pizza delivery. Hiro Protagonist delivers pizza in reality and is a legendary hacker and swordsman in the Metaverse. Y.T., a fifteen-year-old skateboard courier, becomes his partner, and a raft of refugees drifts towards the coast.
worlds.conflict: The media and telecom baron L. Bob Rife has found that an ancient Sumerian language worked on the human brain like machine code. He means to use it, through a drug, a virus and a bitmap called Snow Crash, to make people obey. Hiro, Y.T. and Juanita race to find Enki's counter-spell before the Raft reaches the West Coast.
worlds.politics: Anarcho-capitalism taken literally: sovereignty sold as a franchise, law enforced by private security, defence by mercenary armies, intelligence by the Central Intelligence Corporation. The federal government is a paranoid bureaucracy in its own compounds, and Rife owns the network.
worlds.technology: The Metaverse, a shared virtual city whose main Street runs round a black planet, with avatars built by hackers like Hiro; goggles and portable terminals; smartwheel skateboards; the Rat Things, cyborg guard dogs; and a nuclear warhead that Raven carries with him. The Snow Crash virus runs on both computers and brains.
worlds.mood: Satirical, fast and absurd: a pizza-delivery chase that turns into a lecture on Sumerian myth and then into a war on a floating city.
