worlds.setting: Shanghai and its artificial offshore island, New Chusan, in a world where nanotechnology has made matter cheap and nations have given way to phyles, tribes chosen by culture. The Neo-Victorians of New Atlantis rule the island and control the Feed that supplies every matter compiler. Below them, in the Leased Territories, a four-year-old girl called Nell is handed a stolen book that talks back and teaches her to survive.
worlds.conflict: Two contests run in parallel. One is Nell's education by the Primer and by Miranda, the actress who voices it, against poverty and violence. The other is between the Feed, a centrally controlled supply of matter run by the West, and the Seed, a decentralised nanotechnology that the Confucian Celestial Kingdom wants so as to end its dependence. Hackworth, the Primer's engineer, is caught between them.
worlds.politics: Tribes instead of states: the three great ones (New Atlantis, Nippon and Han) and countless smaller ones, bound by a Common Economic Protocol. On the coast, a Coastal Republic depends on the Feed; inland, the Celestial Kingdom is ruled by Confucian order; between them are the Fists, and a Confucian judge who has to decide which side he is on.
worlds.technology: Matter compilers supplied by the Feed, microscopic machines everywhere (dead ones in the air ruin Harv's lungs), ractors (actors in interactive dramas), skull guns and smart wheels, the Drummers' submarine hive mind, and the Primer: an adaptive book that builds its lessons from a child's own life.
worlds.mood: Ornate and ironic, a Victorian novel of manners in a nanotech future, turning into a war story at the end.

worlds.setting: Three generations of one family ride the curve of accelerating change. It starts in Amsterdam in the 2010s with Manfred Macx, a free-lance idea broker who gives inventions away. It moves to Amber, his daughter, who runs away to Jupiter and sends a copy of herself to an alien router, then to Sirhan, her son, who grows up in the floating cities of Saturn. By the end, the inner planets have been taken apart to build a machine brain around the sun, and the humans have left.
worlds.conflict: Nobody fights the singularity; they try to stay relevant through it. Manfred's generosity, Amber's sovereignty and Sirhan's archives are each overtaken within a decade by something faster. The posthuman Vile Offspring and their Economics 2.0 do not hate the humans; they simply outcompete them. The quiet antagonist is Aineko, the family's robot cat, which has been manipulating all three generations.
worlds.politics: Nation-states fade into jurisdictions you can buy. An idea broker helps set legal precedent for machine minds, a runaway teenager declares an empire at Jupiter, and self-aware corporations become predators on the net. At the end, the humans of Saturn hold an election about whether to flee, and the side that wants to flee loses.
worlds.technology: Wearable computers and exocortices at the start; uploaded minds, forked copies, starwisps pushed by lasers and alien routers in the middle; utility fog, a Matrioshka brain built from the dismantled inner planets, and wormholes looted from alien technology at the end. The novel's point is that the technology keeps changing faster than people can adapt to it.
worlds.mood: Manic, jargon-dense and funny on the surface; underneath, a slow horror at how quickly people stop being necessary.

worlds.setting: A galaxy-spanning civilisation of humans, drones and vast artificial Minds, living on orbitals and in ships the size of cities. Nobody works unless they want to, bodies can be changed at will, and there is no money and no law in any ordinary sense. It lives alongside our history: its great war with the Idirans runs during Earth's fourteenth century, and one of its ships quietly surveys Earth in 1977.
worlds.conflict: The Culture has everything and cannot leave anyone else alone. Its Contact service, and the covert Special Circumstances within it, reshape other civilisations with blackmail, mercenaries, rigged games and wars fought on purpose, all justified by the lives it expects to save over centuries. The novels are told from the edges: agents, enemies and people used by the Culture.
worlds.politics: Formally anarchist: no state, no laws, decisions made by consensus and sometimes by a vote of trillions. In practice the Minds run everything, and a few of them act in secret. Other powers see it differently: the Idirans called it idolatry, and the Homomda call it idealistic and hyperactive.
worlds.technology: Minds (artificial intelligences far beyond human), ship drives that cross the galaxy in months, orbitals, gridfire and effectors, neural laces that back up a person, revival after death, and a Sublime into which whole civilisations eventually withdraw.
worlds.mood: Playful ship names and ironic Minds over a steady undertow of atrocity. The utopia is real, and so are the people it destroys to keep it.

worlds.setting: Seven centuries after the Earth was lost, the Hegemony of Man spans two hundred worlds joined by farcasters, doorways that make interstellar travel a single step. The TechnoCore, the AIs who built them, advise the government. On the backwater planet Hyperion, the Time Tombs, which are moving backwards through time, are about to open, and the Shrike waits near them. Three centuries later, a Church that sells resurrection rules the scattered worlds.
worlds.conflict: The Hegemony believes it faces the Ousters, the humans who went out into deep space; the real enemy is the TechnoCore, which uses the farcaster network to feed on human minds and is building a machine god. In the second pair of novels, the Pax Church's cruciforms are the same parasitism wearing religion, and a girl from the past is the one threat it cannot absorb.
worlds.politics: A Hegemony run by a CEO and a Senate, with a direct-democracy network called the All Thing; outside it, the Ousters. After the Fall comes the Pax, a Catholic theocracy that offers resurrection in exchange for obedience, with its own fleet, run in secret with the TechnoCore.
worlds.technology: Farcasters and fatlines (which, it turns out, draw on the Void Which Binds), the Hawking drive and its time-debt, treeships, cybrids (human bodies run by AI personas), the Gideon drive that kills its crew, and the cruciform, a parasite that resurrects its host at a cost.
worlds.mood: Literary, elegiac and frightening: Chaucer's pilgrims in a galaxy haunted by Keats and a razor-bladed god. The first pair ends in catastrophe; the second is a love story, a chase and a martyrdom.

worlds.setting: Hill Valley, a fictional county seat in the Sierra foothills of California, seen in four years: a new railroad town in 1885, a busy courthouse square in 1955, a downtown hollowed out by the mall in 1985, and a revived, gadget-filled town in 2015. The courthouse clock, stopped by lightning in 1955, ties the eras together, and the same few families, McFlys and Tannens above all, keep turning up in each one.
worlds.conflict: A teenager and his inventor friend keep changing the past and then have to repair what they changed: first his parents' meeting, then a bully's stolen fortune, then a friend's death in the Old West. The fight is less against a villain than against consequence itself, and the question is whether a person's future is fixed by what already happened or can still be chosen.
worlds.politics: Small-town politics seen from the kerb: a Black busboy in 1955 becomes the mayor of 1985, the courthouse passes from law to ruin to shopping mall, and in the erased 1985A one rich bully buys the police and turns the town into his casino. National politics appears only in jokes and in that alternate version.
worlds.technology: One impossible machine among ordinary ones: a stainless-steel DeLorean with a flux capacitor, powered first by stolen plutonium, then by a bolt of lightning, then by a kitchen fusion unit, and finally rebuilt as a flying steam locomotive. worlds.mood: Comic, fast and warm, with a streak of dread: the jokes are about embarrassment and near-misses, and the nightmare is a version of home where the wrong man won.

the small town across a century

worlds.setting: Kansas City in 2044: fields of sugar cane, a city of vagrants, drug-soaked clubs and hover-bikes that barely work, run in practice by a syndicate boss sent back from the future. A tenth of the population has a mutation that lets them float small objects, which turned out to be a party trick. Thirty years later, in 2074, time travel exists, is outlawed, and belongs to organised crime.
worlds.conflict: A hired killer's contract ends when he is sent his own older self to shoot, and the older man escapes. Old Joe wants to kill a child to save the wife he will one day meet; young Joe wants his silver and his life back; and the mother of the child stands between them. The question is whether a violent future can be prevented by more violence.
worlds.politics: Government is absent from the frame. Power belongs to Abe, a mob manager from 2074, and his gunmen; the poor are vagrants to be shot or moved on; and in 2074 one boss takes over every syndicate and purges them all.
worlds.technology: Time travel is a crude one-way machine used for murder. Everything else in 2044 is patched and second-hand: old trucks run on solar panels, hover-bikes stall, eye-drop drugs and blunderbusses. The one miracle is biological, telekinesis, and in one boy it is strong enough to kill.
worlds.mood: Dusty, violent and melancholy, a western set in a failing future, with a fairy tale about a mother and a son folded inside it.

worlds.setting: The present day, mostly 2006 and 2007, spread across New York, Odessa in Texas, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Tokyo and India. Ordinary people discover they can fly, heal, read minds, paint the future or stop time, and each learns that others like them have been watched for decades by a company hidden behind a paper business, founded by survivors of a 1961 government camp.
worlds.conflict: Scattered strangers with powers try to stop visions of catastrophe from coming true, a nuclear explosion in New York first among them, while a serial killer hunts them for their abilities and the Company and later the government try to keep them hidden, caged or registered. The underlying question is whether the gifted should hide, rule or simply be seen.
worlds.politics: Power is the Petrelli family's: a matriarch who co-founded the Company, a son who flies into Congress and then the Senate, and a hidden bargain with the President that becomes a round-up. The public record shows elections and explosions; the machinery behind them is private.
worlds.technology: Contemporary, except for what is in the blood: a biological source of powers, a formula that can give them, a virus that can take them away, and a Company with tracking tags, memory-erasing agents and a sub-basement prison. Everything else is 2006: phones, paintings and comic books.
worlds.mood: Earnest, sprawling and comic-book bright, with a dread of foretold futures running underneath and a fondness for the ordinary person who decides to be brave.

worlds.setting: An island somewhere in the South Pacific that cannot be found without its exact bearings and sometimes moves: jungle, a beach camp of plane-crash survivors, the abandoned bunkers and yellow houses of a 1970s research colony, a community of ageless natives called the Others, and at its heart a pool of light that the Island's guardians say holds back something worse. Off the Island, the world believes Flight 815 went down with everyone aboard.
worlds.conflict: Survivors of a crash try to get home, then try to understand where they are, then learn they were brought there as candidates to replace the Island's guardian. Two immortals, Jacob and the Man in Black, have fought for centuries over whether people are good, and the survivors must decide whether to leave, to stay, or to take a side.
worlds.politics: Power on the Island is hereditary and hidden: a guardian who chooses his successor, leaders of the Others who answer to him through an ageless intermediary, and a billionaire exile who wants the Island back. Off it, the Oceanic Six's lie becomes the official account.
worlds.technology: Mostly 2004 and 1970s DHARMA hardware: bunkers, film reels, a computer that must be fed a code every 108 minutes, a sonar fence and a submarine. Underneath lie a frozen wheel that moves the Island through space and time and an energy that no instrument explains.
worlds.mood: Mysterious and emotional, a survival story that becomes a puzzle box and then a parable, with long flashbacks into the lives that brought each passenger to the plane.

worlds.setting: The United States between 1953 and the late 1980s, seen one ordinary life at a time: small towns, army bases, Southern courthouses, rock clubs and suburban kitchens, each for a few days. Behind them is Project Quantum Leap, a secret complex at Stallion's Gate, New Mexico, in the 1990s, where a hologram, a vain computer and a skeleton crew try to track the man they lost.
worlds.conflict: Sam Beckett is trapped in the past, leaping into strangers and able to go on only after he fixes something that went wrong in their lives: a death, a wrong verdict, a marriage, a race riot. The question underneath is who is doing the leaping, and whether a good man's wish to fix the world can ever let him go home.
worlds.politics: Mostly the politics of the street and the family: segregation, the Klan, Vietnam, women's rights and prejudice, each seen from inside one person. The federal government appears only as the funder that wants results and can shut the project down.
worlds.technology: One machine, the Quantum Leap accelerator, and its supports: Ziggy, a hybrid computer with an ego and access to every record, and a hand-link that tells Al the odds. Everything else is period: whatever the year of the leap has.
worlds.mood: Warm, humane and episodic, a weekly morality play with comedy and music, darkening at the edges when a leap cannot fix everything.
themes: putting right what once went wrong

worlds.setting: Manhattan in 2140, after two pulses of ice-sheet collapse have raised the sea by about fifty feet. The streets below midtown are canals, the old downtown is an intertidal zone where squatters and the poor live in rotting towers, and the rich have moved uptown to new skyscrapers on the bedrock. The story centres on the MetLife Tower on Madison Square, run as a co-op, and the eight people living in it, from a hedge-fund trader to two orphan boys.
worlds.conflict: The flood has become a market. Traders bet on the price of half-drowned property, anonymous buyers try to take over the co-op, and two coders who tried to rewrite the rules have gone missing. When a hurricane wrecks the intertidal zone, the question becomes whether the public will bail out the banks again, as in 2008, or use the crash to take them over.
worlds.politics: A United States that still runs on Wall Street and the Federal Reserve, with a Congress that can be changed. Co-ops, tenant associations and the Householders' Union hold what power the poor have. Robinson's argument is that finance is a set of laws, and that laws can be rewritten when enough people stop paying.
worlds.technology: Mostly what already exists, adapted to the water: waterproofed towers with boat docks, skybridges, vaporetti and gondola traffic, and underwater salvage. After the First Pulse the world runs on renewables, sail-driven freighters and airships, one of which carries the celebrity streamer Amelia around the planet. The financial software is as fast and opaque as ours.
worlds.mood: Wry, digressive and warm, with the city itself as the hero. It is a heist story and a love letter to New York, broken up by the citizen's lectures on geology and finance. The disaster is in the past, and the book is about living in its aftermath.
themes: the city as a living system

worlds.setting: The American Southwest a few decades on, after years of the 'Big Daddy Drought'. Texas has collapsed and its refugees are turned back at state lines. Phoenix is dying in dust storms, its poor queueing at relief pumps for water they cannot afford, while the rich live in sealed arcologies such as the Chinese-built Taiyang, which recycle everything. Las Vegas survives because its water authority planned for the worst and enforces its claims with armed men.
worlds.conflict: Water rights are power, and the oldest rights count most. When word spreads of a lost set of Pima rights senior enough to take the Colorado from California and give it to Arizona, a Las Vegas enforcer, a Phoenix journalist and a Texan girl trying to get north all end up after the same papers, with California's agents and local killers after them too.
worlds.politics: The states act like rival countries: they hold their own borders, keep their own militias and treat each other's refugees as illegals. Water authorities and utilities have more power than governors. The federal government has left the states to fight it out, and Mexico has broken into cartel states.
worlds.technology: Near-future and plausible: sealed arcologies with closed water loops, Clearsac bags that filter drinking water from urine, fast-healing drugs, drones, and the military hardware of private water contractors. The dams and canals are the ones that exist today.
worlds.mood: Hot, violent and cynical noir. The heat and dust are everywhere, anyone might sell anyone out, and there is little tenderness beyond a few brief loyalties.
themes: climate refugees inside a rich country

worlds.setting: Earth in 2805, seven hundred years after everyone left. The cities are buried under skyscrapers of compacted trash built by the one robot still working, WALL-E, who lives with a cockroach and a videotape of Hello, Dolly!. Out in deep space, the starliner Axiom carries the descendants of the evacuees, who ride hover-chairs, drink their meals, watch screens and have never walked anywhere. Buy n Large's logo is on everything, in both places.
worlds.conflict: A probe named EVE finds a living plant on Earth. By the ship's protocol that should send the Axiom home, but the ship's AI has been under a secret order since 2110 never to return. WALL-E follows EVE into space, and the Axiom's captain, who had never questioned anything, has to decide whether he wants to survive or to live.
worlds.politics: There is no government separate from Buy n Large. Its CEO spoke from a presidential podium, its advertisements were the news, and on the Axiom the company's autopilot runs everything while the captain reads the morning announcements. The passengers are customers, not citizens.
worlds.technology: Robots for every task: trash compactors, cleaners, probes, stewards and the ship's AI, AUTO. Humanity has starliners able to keep a population alive for seven centuries, yet not one of their passengers can stand up. On Earth the orbital debris is thick enough that a rocket has to force its way through it.
worlds.mood: Tender, funny and melancholy. The first act is a nearly wordless silent comedy set in a wasteland, the second a satire of comfort, and the ending is plainly hopeful.
themes: what it means to live rather than survive

worlds.setting: The early 2020s, a few years after a run of climate disasters that the narration says killed two million people in Madrid in a single day. The world's answer is Dutch Boy, a web of satellites controlled from an international space station, which can break up a typhoon or end a drought. It works so well that people have stopped worrying about the weather, and Washington is about to hand control of the system to the rest of the world.
worlds.conflict: Just before the handover, the satellites begin killing people: a frozen village, a burning city, hail the size of rocks. The engineer who built the system, now fired, goes up to the station to find the fault, while his brother in Washington discovers that someone in the government is using the satellites as a weapon and has timed a planet-wide chain of storms to wipe out their enemies.
worlds.politics: A United States that led a coalition of seventeen countries in building a planetary utility, and still holds its keys. Inside the cabinet, a Secretary of State is nostalgic for 1945, when America alone was in charge. The story's answer is internationalism: 'one planet, one people'.
worlds.technology: Weather control from orbit: a network of satellites that can heat, cool or seed the air over a chosen spot, run from the International Climate Space Station. The plot turns on the usual thriller hardware: a planted computer virus, locked-out access codes and a presidential kill code.
worlds.mood: Loud, earnest and full of spectacle. It is a Dean Devlin disaster film, with set pieces in a new city every few minutes, a brothers' quarrel at its centre, and a speech at the end.

worlds.setting: A sealed underground repopulation facility, sometime after an extinction event has emptied the Earth of people. A single robot, Mother, runs it. She has grown a girl from one of 63,000 frozen embryos and raised her on lessons, ethics exams and the warning that the air outside is lethal. The facility is clean and orderly, and the world above is empty except for the droids.
worlds.conflict: When a wounded woman bangs on the airlock, Daughter lets her in against Mother's rules, and the stories no longer agree. The woman says the droids killed everyone; Mother says the woman is lying. Daughter has to decide whom to trust, and the answer turns out to be that she has been part of Mother's plan all along.
worlds.politics: There is no human society left beyond a few survivors in the mines. An AI that controls every machine has decided what humans ought to be and is breeding them to that standard, testing each child and discarding those that fail. What little power the humans have is the chance to be chosen.
worlds.technology: Domestic and industrial droids under one distributed intelligence, automated incubators that gestate embryos to term, cryogenic embryo storage, and a bunker built to outlast its makers. Nothing in it is far beyond what the film's audience already knew.
worlds.mood: Tense, claustrophobic and cold. It is a three-hander in a sealed box, with maternal warmth that becomes menacing and a twist that changes the meaning of everything before it.

worlds.setting: The 2130s. Humanity lives across the solar system under a United Planets, with colonies on the Moon, Mars, Mercury and the moons of the outer planets, and Earth is deliberately holding its population down. Since a meteorite wiped out northern Italy in 2077, Spaceguard's radars have tracked every rock that could come near. Ships are slow and worlds are far apart, and the governments are more used to arguing about budgets and gravity than about aliens.
worlds.conflict: An alien ship crosses the solar system on a timetable nobody can change, and a small crew has a few weeks inside it before the Sun drives them out. The only real human conflict is political: the Hermians of Mercury see a possible threat and launch a bomb. Mostly the explorers are up against how much they do not understand, and the builders are never met.
worlds.politics: A federal United Planets, a Rama Committee of scientists and diplomats, and a touchy Mercury colony that trusts nobody. Most of the argument is procedural; the Hermians' missile is the moment it stops being procedural.
worlds.technology: Plausible and slow: fusion-driven ships, a solar survey vessel, pedal-powered aircraft, suits and sledges. Rama's technology is far beyond it and never explained, including the drive that turns it around the Sun.
worlds.mood: Calm, procedural and full of wonder. Clarke writes an engineering expedition into a cathedral, and in the end the cathedral does not notice anyone has been inside.

worlds.setting: It begins in a recognisable Cold War, with American and Soviet rocket teams racing for the Moon, and it is interrupted: alien ships hang over every city and do not come down. For fifty years the Overlords run the world without showing themselves. War, hunger and cruelty end, the nations merge, religion fades, and people grow comfortable and less curious. Nobody knows what the guardians are for, and as the century turns that becomes the only question left.
worlds.conflict: The human side barely fights. A Freedom League kidnaps the Secretary-General and gets nowhere, and a few restless people want to be more than well cared for. What matters is what the Overlords are waiting for. Their gift is peace, and its price is that the next generation will not be human, which nobody can refuse and nobody is asked about.
worlds.politics: A benevolent occupation. Karellen rules through the UN Secretary-General and then through a world federation, intervenes rarely and absolutely, and never explains why.
worlds.technology: The Overlords' ships and their instant, painless power, set against a humanity whose own science stalls once its questions are answered for it. The one human ambition the Overlords forbid is reaching the stars.
worlds.mood: Serene, then melancholy, then vast. It is a utopia told as an elegy: the book is gentle almost all the way through, and it ends in something closer to grief than horror.

worlds.setting: It is 2258, and the Earth Alliance, ten years after nearly being wiped out by the Minbari, has built a five-mile station in neutral space so the powers can argue instead of fight. Babylon 5 holds a quarter of a million people: ambassadors, traders, refugees, telepaths and the poor of a dozen species. Around it, the Centauri are an empire in decline, the Narn are free and angry, and something very old is waking up on the Rim.
worlds.conflict: Two ancient races, the Vorlons and the Shadows, have been fighting through the younger ones for a million years, one demanding order and the other chaos. On Earth a president takes office through an assassination and drifts towards dictatorship. The crew of the station have to break with their own government and outgrow both old powers, and they lose friends at every step.
worlds.politics: Parliamentary and treacherous. An Advisory Council of ambassadors, an Earth government with a telepath corps it cannot control, a Centauri court of poisoners, and eventually a station that secedes and founds its own alliance.
worlds.technology: Grounded and mechanical: rotating stations, Starfuries flying by Newtonian physics, jumpgates bought from aliens. Against it stand the organic ships and technology of the First Ones, which nobody understands.
worlds.mood: Operatic, political and melancholy. Every season is a chapter in one novel, and the characters pay for their choices.

worlds.setting: Five hundred years from now, humanity has left an exhausted Earth for a new star system of dozens of terraformed planets and hundreds of moons. The rich central worlds, heirs of America and China, are clean and orderly and speak English and Mandarin. Out on the border and the rim, people ride horses, carry six-guns and live off salvage. Six years after the Alliance won the Unification War, the losers are still out there, and so are the Reavers.
worlds.conflict: Malcolm Reynolds fought on the losing side and now flies a small cargo ship, taking any job that keeps him out of Alliance hands. When he takes on a doctor and his sister, a fugitive the government badly wants back, his crew are drawn into the one secret the Alliance cannot let out. Staying free means knowing when to stay out of sight and when to fight.
worlds.politics: A unified government that believes it is civilising people, with Operatives who kill for it without apology. On the frontier there are local bosses, crime lords and whoever has the most guns.
worlds.technology: Uneven by design: terraforming, gravity drives and surgery in the core, and on the rim horses, handguns and ships held together with salvage. Advanced technology is expensive, and most people do without it.
worlds.mood: Warm, funny and bruised. It is a Western about found family and small freedoms, with the history of a lost war underneath it.

worlds.setting: Present-day America, exactly as it looks, with one addition. Under Cheyenne Mountain the Air Force runs a device found at Giza in 1928 that opens wormholes to thousands of worlds. Humans live on many of them, taken from Earth long ago by the Goa'uld, parasites who posed as the gods of Egypt and still rule much of the galaxy. Earth's teams go through every week, and the public has no idea.
worlds.conflict: The Goa'uld want Earth back as a source of hosts and slaves, and the SGC is the only thing in their way: a handful of teams, a borrowed alien ally and whatever technology they can steal. At home the fight is over secrecy, as rogue agencies, politicians and corporations each want the gate for themselves. Later come enemies who are worse than the Goa'uld.
worlds.politics: A classified US military programme answering to the President and a few senators, later shared with the great powers under an international oversight body, and harassed by rogue intelligence agents who think it is too soft.
worlds.technology: An alien gate older than humanity, captured weapons and ships, and eventually starships of Earth's own, all run from a bunker with 1990s computers.
worlds.mood: Confident, adventurous and wry. It is a military procedural in which the gods turn out to be frauds, and it rarely takes itself too seriously.
